title: The Year of the Elephant
subtitle: The year Abraha marched on the House, and the year he was born
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1, pp. 43-54 and 158 — Abraha, al-Qulays, the elephant, the birds, and the birth in the Year of the Elephant
Seerah: Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (ed. Ihsan Abbas, Dar Sader), vol. 1, pp. 100-101 — the differing reports on the day of his birth
Qur'an 105 (Surah Al-Fil) — the companions of the elephant

chapters.heading: Abraha's Army and the Falling Birds
chapters.body: In the year the Prophet ﷺ was born, Abraha al-Ashram, who had taken control of Yemen, built a church in Sana'a (al-Qulays) and wrote to the Negus that he would not stop until he had diverted the Arabs' pilgrimage to it. When Abraha learned that a man of Kinana had gone into the church and done something in it, he swore to march on the House and demolish it, and set out with an elephant (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, pp. 43-45). His men seized two hundred camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib, then the chief of Quraysh; when Abd al-Muttalib came to speak with Abraha he asked only for his camels, and Abraha said he had admired him at first sight but thought less of him now that he spoke of camels and not of the House he had come to destroy. Abd al-Muttalib answered: 'I am the owner of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it' (vol. 1 pp. 48-50). He told Quraysh to leave Makkah for the mountain passes, took hold of the ring of the Kaaba's door and prayed, then let it go and went up with them (vol. 1 pp. 50-52). When Abraha's men turned the elephant toward Makkah it knelt and would not rise (vol. 1 p. 52). The Qur'an compressed the end of that march into five verses: 'Have you not considered, [O Muhammad], how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plan into misguidance? And He sent against them birds in flocks, Striking them with stones of hard clay, And He made them like eaten straw' (105:1-5). Ibn Hisham's account has birds coming from the sea, each carrying three stones, the army fleeing and dying along the roads, and Abraha himself dying at Sana'a (vol. 1, pp. 53-54). Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet ﷺ was born on a Monday, the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal, in the Year of the Elephant (vol. 1, p. 158). The early reports differ on the day: Ibn Sa'd records the tenth of Rabi' al-Awwal, from Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali, and the second, from Abu Ma'shar, besides the twelfth (vol. 1 pp. 100-101). The House that had been defended that year is the House that would become the qiblah of the world.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Allah defended His House with birds. What big threat in your life might look smaller if you remembered Who is defending you?

title: The Orphan of Makkah
subtitle: Amina's son, Halimah's milk, Abu Talib's shadow
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1, pp. 158-179 — the birth, the fosterage with Banu Sa'd, Amina's death, Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Talib
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1, pp. 162-165 — Halimah's account of the fosterage (Ibn Ishaq, through a chain with a gap; not from the six books)
Seerah: Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (ed. Ihsan Abbas, Dar Sader), vol. 1, pp. 98-100 and 118-119 — the death of Abdullah; the death of Abd al-Muttalib
Sahih Muslim 162 — the washing of his chest as a boy (Anas)
Qur'an 93:6 — 'Did He not find you an orphan and give [you] refuge?'

chapters.heading: The Child Who Brought Blessing
chapters.body: Muhammad ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant, son of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Amina bint Wahb. Ibn Ishaq has Abdullah die while Amina was still pregnant (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 158). Ibn Sa'd calls that the best established account, and also records one from Hisham ibn al-Kalbi that Abdullah died when the child was twenty-eight months old, or seven months (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 1 pp. 98-100). Abd al-Muttalib looked for wet nurses and a woman of Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr, Halimah bint Abi Dhu'ayb, took him. In her own account, it was a year of drought; her old she-camel gave no milk and her own milk was too little for her son. After she took the orphan, her breasts gave milk, the camel's udder was full, and her donkey outpaced the caravan (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, pp. 162-164; Ibn Ishaq passes it on from Abdullah ibn Ja'far through a chain with a gap, and it is not from the six books). Some months after she took him home to Banu Sa'd, her own son came running to say that two men in white had laid 'our Qurayshi brother' down and opened his belly; Halimah and her husband found him standing with a pale face. A hadith from Anas tells of this event: as a boy, while playing with other children, he was seized by Jibril, who opened his chest, took out a clot of blood saying 'that was the part of Satan in you', and washed his heart with Zamzam water in a golden basin; the children ran to his nurse saying that Muhammad had been killed (Sahih Muslim 162). Afraid for him, Halimah brought him back to Amina, who asked why she had returned him when she had been so eager to keep him (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 pp. 164-165). At six, his mother Amina died at al-Abwa, between Makkah and Madinah, on the way back from visiting his maternal kin in Madinah. He stayed with his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib, for whom a cushion was set in the shade of the Kaaba; his sons sat around it and none sat on it, but the boy would come and sit on it, and when his uncles pulled him away Abd al-Muttalib told them to leave his son alone and sat him beside him. Ibn Ishaq says Abd al-Muttalib died when the Prophet ﷺ was eight (vol. 1 p. 169), and a report in Ibn Sa'd has the Prophet ﷺ himself answer, when asked whether he remembered Abd al-Muttalib's death, 'Yes, I was eight years old' (vol. 1 p. 118). Abu Talib then took charge of his affairs (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 179). The Qur'an would one day name his condition over him: 'Did He not find you an orphan and give [you] refuge?' (93:6). As a reflection: orphanhood was his first teacher; protection was his Lord's first gift.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ lost his parents as a small child and was still raised with love. Who shelters the vulnerable people around you — and could that be you?

title: Al-Amin, The Trustworthy
subtitle: The honest young man the Quraysh could not bribe
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 187-190 and 198 — Maysarah, the marriage, al-Amin
Seerah: Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (ed. Ihsan Abbas, Dar Sader), vol. 1 pp. 129-132 and vol. 8 pp. 16-17 — Nafisa bint Munya; the ages at the marriage
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — Khadijah's testimony to his character

chapters.heading: The Merchant of Makkah
chapters.body: As a young man Muhammad ﷺ was known among Quraysh for the truth of his speech and his great trustworthiness, and Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a woman of standing who hired men to trade with her wealth, sent him to Syria with her slave Maysarah on better terms than she gave other merchants (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 188). The goods sold for double or close to it. Maysarah told her what he had seen, including, in his report, two angels shading Muhammad ﷺ from the sun; that is Maysarah's report as Ibn Ishaq passes it on, not a hadith. Khadijah then sent to him and said that she wished to marry him because of his kinship, his standing among his people, his trustworthiness, his good character and the truth of his speech (p. 189); in Ibn Sa'd's account, which he takes from Nafisa bint Munya herself, Nafisa was the go-between (vol. 1 pp. 129-131). Ibn Hisham gives his age as twenty-five at the marriage (p. 187). Ibn Sa'd, on the authority of al-Waqidi, gives hers as forty (vol. 1 pp. 131-132), while another report in the same book, from Ibn Abbas through Hisham ibn al-Kalbi, makes her twenty-eight (vol. 8 pp. 16-17). Years later, when revelation first shook him, her answer named the character of his whole youth: 'Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your kin, you carry the burdens of the weak, you give to the one who has nothing, you honor the guest, and you help in the calamities that befall in the cause of truth' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3). And Ibn Hisham notes that before revelation Quraysh called him al-Amin, the Trustworthy (p. 198).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Khadijah listed five habits that proved his character. Which of the five — kin, the weak, the destitute, guests, standing with truth — needs your work this month?

title: The Cave of Hira
subtitle: Ramadan, the cave, and the first word
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 235-236 — the yearly retreat to Hira and the month of the first revelation
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — Aisha's narration of the first revelation
Sahih al-Bukhari 3851 — revelation began when he was forty (Ibn Abbas)
Qur'an 96:1-5 — the first revealed words

chapters.heading: Solitude Before the Storm
chapters.body: Before revelation he used to go into seclusion in the cave of Hira, worshipping there for a number of nights at a time, taking provisions with him and returning to Khadijah for more (Sahih al-Bukhari 3). Ibn Ishaq adds, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, that he spent a month there every year, which Quraysh counted as an act of devotion, and fed the poor who came to him; when the month ended he would first circle the Kaaba seven times before going home; and the year Allah chose to honor him with the message the month was Ramadan (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 pp. 235-236). In the month of Ramadan, in the year he turned forty, revelation began; Ibn Abbas gives his age as forty (Sahih al-Bukhari 3851). The angel came to him and said: Iqra — Read. He answered: I am not one who can read. The angel took hold of him and pressed him until he could bear no more, released him and repeated the command — three times — until the words descended: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created - Created man from a clinging substance. Recite, and your Lord is the most Generous - Who taught by the pen - Taught man that which he knew not' (96:1-5). The first word of the final revelation was not a command to rule or to fight. It was a command to read, in the name of the One who created — and among the first things it says of that Lord is that He is the Most Generous (96:3).
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: Khadijah's Test
chapters.body: He returned from the cave with his heart trembling, asked to be covered, and told Khadijah what had happened; her response is preserved in Bukhari's Sahih: 'Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your kin, you carry the burdens of the weak, you give to the one who has nothing, you honor the guest, and you help in the calamities that befall in the cause of truth' (Bukhari 3). Notice how she reasons: from his character to the conclusion that Allah would not disgrace him. Then she took him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal, an old man, blind by then, who had become a Christian before Islam and used to write out the Gospel in Hebrew; he heard the description and said: 'This is the same one who keeps the secrets whom Allah had sent to Moses' (Bukhari 3). The first person the Prophet ﷺ confided in was his wife, and the first confirmation came from her cousin, a man who knew the earlier scriptures. Waraqa added that he wished he were young enough to be alive when his people drove him out, and that no one had ever come with the like of this without being treated as an enemy (Bukhari 3). Soon after, he died, and the revelation paused for a while.

familyQuestion: The first command of the final revelation was Iqra — Read. What is your relationship with reading — and could one good book change your family's next year?

title: Three Years of Whispers
subtitle: The secret call — the first believers
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1, pp. 240, 245-250 and 262 — the private preaching, the first believers
Qur'an 26:214 — 'warn, [O Muhammad], your closest kindred'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4770 — the call from Safa and Abu Lahab

chapters.heading: The Call and the Feast
chapters.body: Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet ﷺ kept his mission hidden for three years, 'according to what reached me', until Allah ordered him to make it public. Ibn Hisham gives Khadijah, who is described as the first to believe in Allah and His Messenger, and then Ali, Zayd ibn Haritha and Abu Bakr their own sections, in that order (the order of the early converts is discussed in the sources). When the command came — 'warn, [O Muhammad], your closest kindred' (26:214) — Muhammad ﷺ climbed Safa and called out to the clans of Quraysh until they gathered, and asked them: if I told you that horsemen in the valley were about to attack you, would you believe me? They said: yes, we have never known you to say anything but the truth. He said: then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment. Abu Lahab cursed him and asked whether he had gathered them for this, and Surah al-Masad (111:1-5) was revealed (Bukhari 4770).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Among the first believers were a woman, a boy and a freed slave. What does that tell you about whose hearts Allah chooses first?

title: Bilal and the Heavy Sand
subtitle: The slave who taught the world a word: Ahad
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 317-320 — the torture of the oppressed; Bilal; Abu Bakr frees six more; the family of Yasir

chapters.heading: Ahad, Ahad
chapters.body: When the call went public and Quraysh could not bribe or debate it down, they turned on believers who had no clan to shield them. Ibn Ishaq says they tortured the oppressed with beating, hunger, thirst and the heat of Makkah's sand (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 317). Bilal's master was Umayyah ibn Khalaf; at midday Bilal was laid on his back in the valley of Makkah with a great rock on his chest and told he would stay so until he died or denied Muhammad ﷺ, and he kept saying: Ahad, Ahad — One, One (p. 318). Abu Bakr told Umayyah to fear Allah, and offered him a stronger black slave of his own in exchange; Umayyah accepted and Abu Bakr freed Bilal. Ibn Hisham lists six others whom Abu Bakr freed on Islam before he emigrated, among them Amir ibn Fuhayra, Umm Ubays and Zunayra (p. 318). He also tells of Ammar, his father and his mother, whom Banu Makhzum took out at midday and tortured on the burning ground of Makkah (pp. 319-320). As a reflection: the weak of Makkah are remembered because the truth did not need the strong to survive. It needed the sincere.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Bilal had one word under a boulder: Ahad. If your faith cost you comfort today, what would your one word be?

title: The Night of the Journey
subtitle: Al-Isra wal-Mi'raj — five prayers as the gift of the heavens
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 349 — the ascent and the reduction of the prayers from fifty to five (Abu Dharr)
Qur'an 17:1 — 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night'
Sahih Muslim 162 — Bayt al-Maqdis, the heavens and the prophets met in them, the Lote Tree, and the reduction of the prayers (Anas)

chapters.heading: From the Haram to the Farthest Mosque
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ was carried from the sacred mosque to the farthest mosque in a single night: 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed' (17:1). In the narration of Anas in Sahih Muslim he was brought the Buraq, came to Bayt al-Maqdis and prayed two rak'ahs there, and was then taken up through the heavens: Adam at the first, Isa and Yahya at the second, Yusuf at the third, Idris at the fourth, Harun at the fifth, Musa at the sixth, and Ibrahim at the seventh, leaning against the Bayt al-Ma'mur; then to the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Muslim 162). The narration of Abu Dharr in Bukhari 349 names Adam, Idris, Musa, Isa and Ibrahim, and places Ibrahim in the sixth heaven, so the reports differ on where each prophet was met. Musa asked him at the end what his nation had been given, and when he heard fifty prayers a day, Musa said: your people cannot bear fifty — go back and ask your Lord to lighten it (Bukhari 349, Muslim 162). He returned and returned again, until the covenant stood at five prayers for the reward of fifty. In Bukhari 349 the word came: these are five and they are fifty, My word does not change; in Muslim 162 the five prayers are each credited as ten, so that they make fifty. As a reflection: the five daily prayers are not a burden negotiated down. They are a gift negotiated up — from the Lord of the heavens, through Musa's concern for the believers, to your doorstep five times a day.

familyQuestion: Five prayers were gifted from above the seven heavens. Do you treat them as a burden negotiated down — or a gift you get to keep?

title: The Boycott
subtitle: Shut in a ravine by a written covenant, and a document eaten by termites
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1, pp. 350-352 and 374-377 — the document of the boycott and its undoing
Seerah: Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (ed. Ihsan Abbas, Dar Sader), vol. 1, pp. 208-210 — the hardship in the ravine and how long it lasted

chapters.heading: A Document Against a Clan
chapters.body: When persuasion and pressure had not worked, Quraysh tried isolation. Ibn Ishaq records that they gathered and agreed a covenant against Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib: no one would marry into them or give them women in marriage, and no one would sell to them or buy from them. They wrote it in a document and hung it inside the Kaaba to make it binding (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, p. 350). Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib gathered around Abu Talib in his shi'b, the ravine where they were shut in, while Abu Lahab, of Banu Hashim, left them and sided with Quraysh (vol. 1, p. 351). Hisham ibn Amr, whose family ties on his mother's side were with Banu Hashim, would bring a camel loaded with food to the mouth of the ravine at night, take off its halter, strike its flank and let it run in to them (vol. 1 p. 375). Then he went to Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayya, al-Mut'im ibn Adi, Abu al-Bakhtari and Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, one by one, until they agreed to meet by night above Makkah to undo the document. Zuhayr circled the Kaaba seven times and vowed not to sit down until the cruel document was torn; Abu Jahl called him a liar. When al-Mut'im went to tear it, he found that termites had eaten it except for the words 'bismika Allahumma' (in Your name, O God) (vol. 1, pp. 375-376). Another report in the same book, given on the word of 'some people of knowledge', has the Prophet ﷺ tell Abu Talib that Allah had sent termites against the document so that they left every mention of Allah in it and ate away the injustice, the cutting of ties and the falsehood; Abu Talib went to Quraysh and said that if it was as his nephew had said they must stop, and if not he would hand his nephew over to them. They agreed, looked, and found it as the Prophet ﷺ had said, which, Ibn Hisham says, only made them worse; it was then that the group acted to undo the document (vol. 1 p. 377). Ibn Sa'd says Quraysh cut off their supplies, so that they could go out only from one pilgrimage season to the next, until the hardship reached them and the crying of their children was heard from beyond the ravine (vol. 1 p. 208). He gives three years for their stay, and the tenth year of the mission for their coming out, but also records a report from Muhammad ibn Ali that the Prophet ﷺ and his family stayed two years, so the length is not agreed (vol. 1 pp. 208-210).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The boycott cut a whole clan off from trade and marriage, and it broke before their loyalty did. What pressure are you under that only feels permanent?

title: The First Hijrah
subtitle: Abyssinia — the king who wept at Surah Maryam and refused to hand them over
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1, pp. 321-323 and 333-338 — the emigration to Abyssinia, the envoys, Ja'far before the Negus

chapters.heading: A Kingdom That Let Them Pray
chapters.body: When the suffering of his companions was more than he could shield them from, the Prophet ﷺ told them, as Ibn Ishaq reports: go to the land of Abyssinia, for there is a king there under whom no one is wronged — a land of truth — until Allah grants you relief (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, p. 321). It was the first emigration in Islam (vol. 1 p. 322). Ibn Ishaq names ten who left first, among them Uthman ibn Affan with his wife Ruqayya, the Prophet's ﷺ daughter, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Mus'ab ibn Umayr, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, and Abu Salama with his wife Umm Salama; Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and many others followed until they had gathered there (vol. 1 pp. 322-323). No army, no land promised, just a just king. When the emigrants had found safety there, Quraysh sent Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'a and Amr ibn al-As with Makkan leather and other gifts for the Negus and for each of his bishops, with instructions to give each bishop his gift before speaking and to ask for the Muslims to be handed over before they were heard (vol. 1, pp. 333-335, from Umm Salama's account). The Negus took an oath and refused to surrender them without hearing them. He summoned the Muslims and his bishops, who spread their scriptures around him, and asked what religion they had left their people for. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib answered, describing what they had been and what the Messenger ﷺ had called them to, and when the Negus asked if they had anything from Allah, he recited the opening of Surah Maryam. The Negus wept until his beard was wet, the bishops wept until their scriptures were wet, and he said that this and what Isa brought came from one niche. He told the two envoys to go and would not surrender the Muslims to them (vol. 1, pp. 335-337). The next day Amr tried again with a question about Isa; Ja'far answered that he is Allah's servant, His messenger, His spirit and His word, and the Negus took a stick from the ground and said Isa did not exceed what Ja'far had said by the width of that stick; he told the Muslims they were safe in his land, that whoever insulted them would pay a fine, and that he would not want a mountain of gold at the price of harming one of them (vol. 1 pp. 337-338). A Christian kingdom had become the first refuge of Islam.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Negus protected strangers he had no reason to protect. Have you ever been protected by a stranger — or been one for someone else?

title: The Conversion of Umar
subtitle: The man who set out with a sword to kill the Prophet ﷺ came to believe
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 343-346 — Umar's conversion (the account of the narrators of Madinah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3680 — the Prophet's ﷺ dream of Umar's palace in Paradise

chapters.heading: A Lion Changes Direction
chapters.body: Umar ibn al-Khattab set out, girded with his sword, to kill the Prophet ﷺ (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 343). On the way Nu'aym ibn Abdullah, who was secretly Muslim, sent him to his own house first: Khabbab used to visit his sister Fatima bint al-Khattab to teach her the Qur'an, and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd was also a Muslim (pp. 343-344). Umar struck his sister and wounded her; a page headed 'Ta-Ha' was in the house (p. 344). Then, in this account, he washed because she said only the pure may touch it, took the page and read it, and said: how fine this speech is, and how noble (p. 345). Khabbab came out and told him of the Prophet's ﷺ prayer that Islam be strengthened by Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham or by Umar ibn al-Khattab, and said the Prophet was in a house by Safa. Umar took his sword and went to that house and knocked at the door (p. 345). A man in the house who looked through a gap in the door saw him girded with his sword and went back alarmed; Hamza said to let him in, since if he came for good they would welcome it and if for harm they would kill him with his own sword. The Prophet ﷺ went to meet him, took hold of his waist-cloth or the fold of his robe, pulled him sharply and asked what had brought him, saying he did not think Umar would stop until Allah sent a calamity upon him. Umar said: 'I have come to you to believe in Allah and His Messenger and in what has come from Allah.' The Prophet ﷺ said Allahu akbar so loudly that the people in the house knew Umar had become Muslim (p. 346). Ibn Hisham gives this as the account of the narrators of Madinah, and goes on to a different account, from Ata and Mujahid (p. 346). The Prophet's ﷺ dream of a palace in Paradise that he was told was Umar's is in Sahih al-Bukhari 3680.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Umar went to the door with a sword and was met by a page of the Qur'an. When did something you read change the errand you were on?

title: Taif
subtitle: Driven to a vineyard — and he hoped for their descendants
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 419-422 — the journey to Ta'if, the three brothers, the vineyard, the supplication, Addas, Nakhla
Seerah: Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (ed. Ihsan Abbas, Dar Sader), vol. 1 pp. 210-212 — the ten days and the stoning (al-Waqidi's report)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 — the day of Aqabah and the angel of the mountains

chapters.heading: The Saddest Day of the Seerah
chapters.body: After Abu Talib died, Quraysh harmed the Prophet ﷺ more than they had before, and he went out to Ta'if to seek the support of Thaqif (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 419). He went alone and sat with three brothers who were then the chiefs of Thaqif, Abd Yalil, Mas'ud and Habib, sons of Amr, called them to Allah and asked for their help; one answered mockingly, another asked whether Allah had found no one else to send, and the third refused to speak to him at all. He left despairing of Thaqif and asked them to keep it quiet, and they instead set their fools and slaves on him, cursing and shouting at him, until he was driven into a vineyard belonging to Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a (pp. 419-420). There, in Ibn Ishaq's account, he prayed: 'O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my lack of resources and my humiliation before the people... If You are not displeased with me, then I do not care' (p. 420; Ibn Ishaq introduces it with 'as it was told to me', without a full chain). Utba and Shayba, moved to pity, sent their Christian slave Addas with a bunch of grapes; he heard the Prophet ﷺ say 'in the name of Allah' before eating and, learning that Addas was from Nineveh, said it was the town of the righteous man Yunus ibn Matta, 'my brother: he was a prophet and I am a prophet', and Addas kissed his head, hands and feet (p. 421, again 'it was told to me'). In a separate hadith Aisha asks whether he had faced a day harder than Uhud, and he answers that the worst was the day he presented himself to Ibn Abd Yalil ibn Abd Kulal and got no response; he walked on grieving until, at Qarn al-Tha'alib, Jibril and the angel of the mountains offered to crush the people between the two mountains, and he declined, hoping that Allah would bring from their descendants people who worship Allah alone (Bukhari 3231). The hadith itself does not mention stones or the word Ta'if. Ibn Sa'd, relaying al-Waqidi through unnamed narrators, adds that he stayed ten days, that the chiefs told him to leave and set their fools on him, who pelted him with stones until his feet bled while Zayd ibn Haritha shielded him and was wounded in the head (Tabaqat, vol. 1 pp. 211-212). That is a weaker chain than the Bukhari hadith. On the way back at Nakhla seven jinn heard him pray (Ibn Hisham p. 422; Qur'an 46:29).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: He was shouted at and driven out, and still hoped for their descendants. Is there someone who hurt you whose children you could still bless?

title: The Pledges of Aqabah
subtitle: Seventy-five hands in the dark — Madinah accepts the message
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 429, 433, 434 and 441-443 — the six, the twelve, Mus'ab, the second pledge, the twelve leaders
Sahih al-Bukhari 18 — the pledge of Aqabah: no shirk, theft, adultery, killing children, slander or disobedience in good (narrated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit)

chapters.heading: Twelve, Then Seventy-Five
chapters.body: At the pilgrimage season the Prophet ﷺ met six men of the Khazraj at Aqabah, among them As'ad ibn Zurara and Rafi' ibn Malik. Ibn Ishaq says they told one another that this was the prophet the Jews had threatened them with, and that they had left a people among whom there was enmity and evil, hoping Allah would unite them through him (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 429). The next year twelve men met him at Aqabah. Ubada ibn al-Samit says: 'we were twelve men', and the pledge was the like of the women's pledge, before fighting was prescribed: not to associate anything with Allah, not to steal, not to commit adultery, not to kill their children (p. 433; also Sahih al-Bukhari 18, in the wording: no shirk, theft, adultery, killing children, slander or disobedience in good). The Prophet ﷺ sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr with them, ordering him to teach them the Qur'an and Islam and to give them understanding in the religion; Asim ibn Umar reports that he used to lead them in prayer (p. 434). The next year the pilgrims of Yathrib came again; a narrator says: 'we were seventy-three men, and with us two women', and that they slipped out secretly after a third of the night and gathered in the ravine at Aqabah, where al-Abbas, still on his people's religion, spoke first and asked them to protect his nephew only if they could keep their promise (pp. 441-442). The Prophet ﷺ recited Qur'an, called them to Allah and to Islam, and said: 'I pledge you that you will protect me as you protect your women and children.' Al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur took his hand and swore that they would protect him as they protected their own; Abu al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihan asked whether, if they cut their ties with the Jews and Allah gave him victory, he would return to his own people and leave them. The Prophet ﷺ smiled and said: 'Rather, blood is blood and ruin is ruin; I am of you and you are of me; I will fight those you fight and make peace with those you make peace with' (p. 442). He then asked them to bring out twelve leaders, and they chose nine from the Khazraj and three from the Aws (p. 443). The Ansar of Madinah were preparing a city before the Prophet ﷺ had ever seen it.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Ansar believed in a man they had met twice. What makes someone trustworthy enough to follow?

title: The Hijrah
subtitle: The cave, the companion, and the man who rode for a bounty
sources: Qur'an 9:40 — 'as one of two, when they were in the cave'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 — the Hijrah with Abu Bakr, three nights in the cave on Mount Thawr, Asma, the guide
Sahih al-Bukhari 3653 — Abu Bakr in the cave: 'what do you think of two whose third is Allah'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3906 — Suraqa, the fall of the horse and the written pledge
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 482, 485-486, 489-492 — Quraysh's plan, the cave, Asma, Suraqa, the route, Quba

chapters.heading: The Second of Two
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ left Makkah with Abu Bakr and entered a cave in Mount Thawr, below the city (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 485). Ibn Ishaq, as Ibn Hisham gives it, has Abu Jahl propose that Quraysh take one strong, well-born young man from every clan to strike together, so that Banu Abd Manaf could not fight all of Quraysh and would settle for the blood-price (vol. 1 p. 482). In the cave Abu Bakr's son listened by day to what people said of them, and Asma bint Abi Bakr brought food at nightfall; Ibn Ishaq says that when the travel bag had no strap she cut her waist-belt in two to tie it, which is why she was called Dhat al-Nitaq (pp. 485-486), and Bukhari 3905 uses the title Dhat al-Nitaqayn. Bukhari 3905 has them stay in the cave three nights. In Bukhari 3653 Abu Bakr says that if one of the pursuers looked down at his own feet he would see them, and the Prophet ﷺ answers: what do you think of two whose third is Allah? The Qur'an keeps his words: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us', and says Allah supported him with soldiers you did not see (9:40). Later tradition adds a spider's web and a dove's nest at the entrance; these are not in the Qur'an or in Bukhari 3905, and no chain for them is given here. Ibn Hisham reports Quraysh offering a hundred camels to whoever brought him back (pp. 486, 489). In Suraqa ibn Malik's own account there, his horse stumbled and threw him three times, and the third time its forelegs sank into the ground; he asked for a written pledge, and the Prophet ﷺ told Abu Bakr to write it, on a bone, a scrap or a potsherd (pp. 489-490). Suraqa put it in his quiver, went back and kept silent about what he had seen. Bukhari 3906 also has the horse's forelegs sink and the written pledge. The two reached Quba, among Banu Amr ibn Awf, on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal; Ibn Hisham gives it as the twelfth night, at mid-morning (p. 492). Ibn Sa'd's own report has Ali reaching Quba about mid-Rabi' al-Awwal while the Prophet ﷺ was still there (vol. 3 pp. 22, 228).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Allah's help in the cave came without any visible guard. What unseen help have you only noticed looking back?

title: The Arrival in Madinah
subtitle: The city rejoiced: the Messenger has arrived
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 494-496 — Quba, the first Friday prayer, the camel, Abu Ayyub
Sahih al-Bukhari 3925 — the joy of Madinah at his arrival (al-Bara' ibn Azib)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2048 — Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: half the wealth, 'where is the market?'
Qur'an 9:108 — 'a mosque founded on righteousness from the first day'

chapters.heading: A City That Ran to Meet Him
chapters.body: At Quba the Prophet ﷺ stayed, by Ibn Hisham's account, from Monday to Thursday (Banu Amr ibn Awf claimed he stayed longer) and founded his mosque there, leaving on the Friday and praying the first Friday prayer in Madinah with Banu Salim ibn Awf in the valley of Ranuna (vol. 1 p. 494); the Qur'an honors a mosque 'founded on righteousness from the first day' (9:108). Then he rode toward Madinah. Clan after clan, among them Banu Salim, Banu Bayada, Banu Sa'ida, Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj and Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar, stopped his camel and invited him to stay with them, speaking of their numbers, strength and protection, and each time he answered: 'Let her go her way, for she is commanded' (pp. 494-495). The camel knelt at the gate of the mosque-site in the house of Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar; he did not dismount, it rose, walked a little, then turned back and knelt in the same place, and he got down; Abu Ayyub al-Ansari carried his saddle into his house (pp. 495-496). Al-Bara' ibn Azib said he had never seen the people of Madinah rejoice as they did: even the slave girls were saying that the Messenger of Allah had arrived (Bukhari 3925). The Ansar and Muhajirun were paired as brothers. In one hadith the Ansari Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' offered Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf half of his wealth; Abd al-Rahman declined and asked only where the market was, and the Prophet ﷺ later told him to hold a wedding feast, even with one sheep (Bukhari 2048). The first economy of Madinah, then, began with an offer of half and an answer of 'show me the market'.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Sa'd offered half of everything and Abd al-Rahman asked only for the market. What would you genuinely share, and what would you refuse and still be grateful for?

title: The Charter of Madinah
subtitle: One document between the believers and the Jews of Madinah — each keeping their own religion
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 501-504 — the text of the document between the Muhajirun, the Ansar and the Jews
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 516-517 — the Islam of Abdullah ibn Salam
Qur'an 63:1 — the hypocrites

chapters.heading: Writing a Nation
chapters.body: After the Hijra, Ibn Ishaq says, the Prophet ﷺ wrote a document between the Muhajirun and the Ansar and made a truce with the Jews of Madinah, confirming them in their religion and property. Ibn Ishaq gives the text without a chain of narrators (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, pp. 501-504). It opens in the name of Allah, binds the believers and Muslims of Quraysh and Yathrib and those who follow and fight alongside them, and declares them one community apart from other people. The Jews of Banu Awf are one community with the believers: the Jews have their religion and the Muslims theirs; Jews and believers each bear their own expenses and spend alongside one another while they fight together; they support one another against whoever attacks the people of the document; Yathrib is sacred to them; and any dispute is to be referred to Allah and to Muhammad. The same status is given to a list of other Jewish clans. Abdullah ibn Salam, a learned Jewish rabbi of Madinah, embraced Islam when the Prophet ﷺ arrived (Ibn Ishaq's account, from some of his family, vol. 1 pp. 516-517). The Qur'an says of the hypocrites of Madinah that they would say 'We testify that you are the Messenger of Allah' while Allah testifies that they are liars (63:1). Ibn Hisham also lists Jewish leaders of several clans who were hostile to the Prophet ﷺ, except Abdullah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq (vol. 1, p. 516). This story gives only what the document says; it does not trace what later became of each party. As a reflection: it is an early written covenant for a city of more than one community.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The document let believers and Jews live under one agreement while each kept their own religion. What community are you part of that needs a shared agreement more than a shared belief?

title: The Qibla Changes
subtitle: Sixteen months toward Jerusalem — then one command turned a congregation around
sources: Qur'an 2:142-150 — the whole passage, 'We see the turning of your face'
Qur'an 2:177 — righteousness is not only the direction you face
Sahih al-Bukhari 399 — the change of the qiblah, sixteen or seventeen months (al-Bara' ibn Azib)

chapters.heading: Turning the Whole Community
chapters.body: For sixteen or seventeen months in Madinah the Prophet ﷺ prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), but he loved to face the Ka'bah, so Allah revealed: 'We have certainly seen the turning of your face, [O Muhammad], toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram' (2:144), and he faced the Ka'bah (Bukhari 399, from al-Bara' ibn Azib). The foolish among the people then asked, 'What has turned them away from their qiblah, which they used to face?' and the answer came: 'Say, "To Allah belongs the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path"' (2:142). In the same hadith a man who had prayed with the Prophet ﷺ facing the Ka'bah passed some of the Ansar praying the Asr prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis, told them he had prayed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ facing the Ka'bah, and they turned to the Ka'bah where they stood (Bukhari 399). The Qur'an adds the deeper lesson: righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but belief in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets, and what follows from it (2:177). Where the change happened, and in which prayer, is not stated in this hadith, so this story does not say.

familyQuestion: The Ansar at prayer heard the news and turned where they stood, without arguing. When has your community changed direction without splitting?

title: Badr: The Two Armies Meet
subtitle: A little over three hundred against some nine hundred to a thousand
sources: Qur'an 3:123-126 — 'already had Allah given you victory at' Badr
Qur'an 8:41 — 'the day of criterion - the day when the two armies met'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3959 — the men of Badr, over three hundred and ten (al-Bara')
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 617, 626-627 — the scouts' estimate of Quraysh, Sawad, the plea in the shelter

chapters.heading: The Criterion
chapters.body: The Qur'an later named the day: 'the day of criterion - the day when the two armies met' (8:41). Al-Bara' ibn Azib said the Companions used to say that the men of Badr were a little over three hundred and ten (Bukhari 3959), against Quraysh, whom a scout reported as between nine hundred and a thousand (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 617). On the morning of the battle the Prophet ﷺ was straightening the ranks with an arrow in his hand; he prodded Sawad ibn Ghaziyya in the belly to bring him into line, and Sawad asked to take his retaliation, which the Prophet ﷺ allowed (p. 626). Then, in the shelter built for him, he pleaded with his Lord for the victory promised: 'O Allah, if this band perishes today You will not be worshipped'; Abu Bakr told him that was enough pleading, for Allah would fulfil what He promised (p. 627). The Qur'an records the other side of that morning: 'already had Allah given you victory at' Badr 'while you were few in number' (3:123). It records the promise of three thousand angels, and of five thousand if they stayed patient and conscious of Allah (3:124-125), and says it was only good tidings 'to reassure your hearts thereby. And victory is not except from Allah' (3:126).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Allah sent angels but said victory is only from Him. When you win, who do you thank first?

title: Badr: The Prisoners
subtitle: The prisoners of Badr: 'treat them well'
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 p. 645 — the prisoners distributed; 'treat them well'; Abu Aziz and the bread
Musnad Ahmad — teaching Ansari children to write as ransom (Ibn Abbas); number and grade not verified
Qur'an 8:67-71 — 'It is not for a prophet to have captives'

chapters.heading: Mercy After Victory
chapters.body: The battle was over and the prisoners were taken. Ibn Ishaq reports that the Prophet ﷺ distributed the prisoners among his companions and said: 'Treat the prisoners well' (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 645). Abu Aziz ibn Umayr, one of them, later said that the men who held him gave him the bread at their meals while they ate dates themselves (p. 645). Ibn Abbas is reported to have said that some of the Badr captives had nothing to pay, so the Prophet ﷺ made their ransom teaching Ansari children to write (Musnad Ahmad, from Ibn Abbas; its hadith number and grade were not verified). That report is outside the two Sahihs, so treat it as a report. The revelation that came about the day named the tension honestly: 'It is not for a prophet to have captives [of war] until he inflicts a massacre [upon Allah's enemies] in the land' (8:67), and, 'If not for a decree from Allah that preceded, you would have been touched for what you took by a great punishment' (8:68). But the surah goes on to the law that outlasted the battle: 'So consume what you have taken of war booty' (8:69), and calls it 'lawful and good' — and to the prisoners themselves: 'and He will forgive you' (8:70), if Allah knows good in their hearts.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ told his companions to treat their prisoners well, and they gave them the bread. When did you last do the generous thing for someone who had lost to you?

title: Uhud: The Day the Line Broke
subtitle: Archers leave the pass — and the Prophet ﷺ bleeds on the mountain
sources: Qur'an 3:152-155 — the day 'some of you desired the world'
Qur'an 3:144 — 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4043 — the archers, the order not to leave their place, seventy casualties (al-Bara' ibn Azib)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5722 — the helmet broken, his face bloodied, his incisor broken, Ali and Fatima (Sahl ibn Sa'd)
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 66, 77-79 — the Quraysh cavalry, al-Zubayr's account, what the Prophet ﷺ suffered

chapters.heading: The Turning
chapters.body: At Uhud the Prophet ﷺ placed a company of archers at a set place under Abdullah ibn Jubayr and told them not to leave it, whether they saw the Muslims winning or losing (Bukhari 4043, from al-Bara' ibn Azib). Quraysh came with three thousand men and two hundred horse, with Khalid ibn al-Walid, not yet a Muslim, commanding the right wing of the cavalry and Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl the left (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 66). When the enemy broke and ran, the Muslims began to say 'The booty, the booty!'; Abdullah ibn Jubayr reminded them of the Prophet's order, but his companions refused to stay, and seventy Muslims were lost (Bukhari 4043). In al-Zubayr's account the archers turned toward the camp and left the Muslims' backs open to the cavalry, who attacked from behind, and a cry went up that Muhammad had been killed (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 pp. 77-78). The enemy reached the Prophet ﷺ: he was struck with stones, one of his teeth was broken, his face was cut and his lip wounded, the blow being attributed to Utba ibn Abi Waqqas (vol. 2 p. 79). Sahl ibn Sa'd recalled that his helmet was broken on his head, his face covered with blood and his incisor broken; Ali brought water in his shield and Fatima washed the blood from his face (Bukhari 5722). The Qur'an answered the rumour of his death: 'Muhammad is not but a messenger. [Other] messengers have passed on before him. So if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels [to unbelief]?' (3:144). And it named the cause of the reversal: 'And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing the enemy by His permission until [the time] when you lost courage and fell to disputing about the order [given by the Prophet] and disobeyed after He had shown you that which you love' (3:152). Hamza's death at Uhud is told in the next story.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The archers left the post they had been given when the booty appeared. What 'post' are you tempted to leave right now?

title: Uhud: Hamza and the Women
subtitle: The master of martyrs, the mutilated dead, and Hind's answer
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 91, 95-97 — Hind; the Prophet ﷺ and Hamza; the prohibition of mutilation; Safiyya
Sahih al-Bukhari 4072 — Wahshi's account of killing Hamza
Sahih al-Bukhari 3825 — Hind bint Utba after she embraced Islam
Qur'an 16:126-128 — 'punish with an equivalent of that with which you were harmed'

chapters.heading: The Lion and the Lesson
chapters.body: Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, was killed at Uhud by a thrown spear: Wahshi, a slave of Jubayr ibn Mut'im who had been promised his freedom for it, tells how he drove the spear in (Bukhari 4072). Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet ﷺ went looking for him and found him in the valley with his belly cut open, his liver taken out, his nose and ears cut off (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 95). Ibn Hisham also names Hind bint Utba as the one who made anklets and necklaces from the ears and noses of the dead and who cut into Hamza's liver (p. 91). Ibn Ishaq has the Prophet ﷺ say, seeing him, that were it not for Safiyya's grief and for the precedent it would set, he would leave him for the beasts and the birds (p. 95); and then swear that if Allah gave him victory over Quraysh he would mutilate thirty of their men (pp. 95-96). The Muslims said the same. Then came the revelation: 'punish with an equivalent of that with which you were harmed. But if you are patient - it is better for those who are patient' (16:126). Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of narrators he does not name, says the Prophet ﷺ forgave, was patient and forbade mutilation (p. 96), and Samura ibn Jundub is quoted as saying he never stood to speak without urging charity and forbidding mutilation (p. 96). Hamza's sister Safiyya came to see him; the Prophet ﷺ sent her son al-Zubayr to turn her back, but she said she had heard her brother was mutilated, that it was for Allah's sake, and that she would be patient and hope for reward, so he let her come, and she prayed over him and asked forgiveness for him (p. 97). Hind bint Utba later came to him and said that before she embraced Islam there was no household on earth she wished to see disgraced more than his, and now none she wished to see honored more (Bukhari 3825).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ was told that patience is better than the revenge he had sworn. What revenge habit could your family end with you?

title: The Trench
subtitle: Ten thousand at the walls — and a biting wind from the unseen
sources: Qur'an 33:9-27 — '[Remember] when they came at you from above you and from below you'
Qur'an 33:10-11 — 'there the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking'
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 213-233 — the Battle of the Trench

chapters.heading: The Severe Shaking
chapters.body: Ibn Ishaq dates the Trench to Shawwal of the fifth year (vol. 2 p. 213). Men of Banu al-Nadir and Banu Wa'il went to Makkah and urged Quraysh to fight the Prophet ﷺ, and then to Ghatafan; Quraysh marched under Abu Sufyan, and Ghatafan under chiefs including Uyayna ibn Hisn and al-Harith ibn Awf (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, pp. 215-216). The Prophet ﷺ ordered a trench dug around Madinah and worked on the digging himself; some hypocrites hung back and slipped away to their families without leave. When the Quraysh horsemen saw the trench they said it was a stratagem the Arabs had not used; Ibn Hisham adds that it is said Salman the Persian suggested the trench (vol. 2, p. 224). Quraysh camped at Majma' al-Asyal with their Ahabish and the tribes that followed them, ten thousand by Ibn Ishaq's count, while Ghatafan and the men of Najd camped by Uhud; the Prophet ﷺ and about three thousand Muslims set their backs to Sal' with the trench between them and the enemy (vol. 2 pp. 219-220). As the siege tightened and fear spread, a man named Mu'attib ibn Qushayr said: Muhammad used to promise us the treasures of Kisra and Caesar, and today none of us feels safe going out to relieve himself (vol. 2, p. 222). Ibn Hisham adds that a scholar he trusted told him Mu'attib was not a hypocrite, since he had fought at Badr (p. 222). There was little fighting beyond arrows and a blockade, though a few Quraysh horsemen forced their horses across a narrow part of the trench and Ali killed Amr ibn Abd Wudd (vol. 2, pp. 223-225). The Qur'an preserved the city at its breaking point: '[Remember] when they came at you from above you and from below you, and when eyes shifted [in fear], and hearts reached the throats and you assumed about Allah [various] assumptions. There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking' (33:10-11). Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud came to the Prophet ﷺ and said he had become Muslim but his people did not know; the Prophet ﷺ told him to sow discord among the enemy if he could, and he went to Banu Qurayza (vol. 2, p. 229). Then Allah sowed discord among the allies, and sent a very cold wind on a winter night that overturned their pots and threw down their tents; Abu Sufyan called on Quraysh to leave, and Ghatafan turned back for their own land (vol. 2, pp. 231-233; the Qur'an mentions the wind and the soldiers in 33:9). The Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims returned to Madinah. Madinah had not won the Trench by arms alone: the Qur'an credits Allah with sending the wind (33:9).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The trench held because Salman, a Persian outsider, was listened to. Whose 'outsider' idea are you ignoring right now?

title: Hudaybiyyah
subtitle: The treaty that looked like defeat — and the sura named a clear conquest
sources: Qur'an 48:1-3 — 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest'
Sahih al-Bukhari 2731-2732 — the terms of the treaty of Hudaybiyyah and Umar's objection
Sahih al-Bukhari 4153-4154 — about fourteen hundred (or fifteen hundred) men (Jabir)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4177 — a sura revealed on the journey (Al-Fath)
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 316-319 — the truce, the ten years, Umar's question and the reply, Abu Jandal

chapters.heading: The Clear Conquest
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ set out for Makkah to perform umrah in peace with about fourteen hundred men (Bukhari 4154, from Jabir; Bukhari 4153 has Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab relating that Jabir also said fifteen hundred) — and Quraysh barred them from the House at Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari 2731). The treaty that followed looked like surrender. Quraysh insisted that he go back that year (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 316). In the text Ibn Hisham gives, the two sides agreed to put war away from the people for ten years, in which people would be safe; and a man of Quraysh who came to Muhammad without his guardian's permission would be returned, while one who went to Quraysh would not (p. 317). Bukhari 2731 has the same clause that Suhayl demanded, even if the man had embraced Islam. Umar ibn al-Khattab could not bear it. In Bukhari 2731 he asks whether their cause is not the right one and the enemy's wrong. In Ibn Hisham he asks: why should we accept humiliation in our religion? And the Prophet ﷺ answers: 'I am the servant of Allah and His Messenger; I will not disobey His command, and He will not let me be lost' (p. 317). Bukhari 4177 records that on a night journey he said a sura had been revealed to him that night that was dearer to him than everything the sun rises on, and recited 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest' (48:1), the opening of the sura of Al-Fath; Bukhari files it under the Hudaybiyyah expedition. The Qur'an named what no eye could see: 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest' (48:1). Two years later the Muslims entered Makkah.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The treaty everyone hated opened the doors of Arabia. Have you ever had a 'defeat' that was actually a door?

title: The Letters to the Rulers
subtitle: The letter that reached the Emperor of Rome
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 p. 607 — the envoys and the kings they were sent to
Sahih al-Bukhari 2941 — the letter to Heraclius and Abu Sufyan's questioning
Sahih al-Bukhari 64 — Kisra tears the letter (Ibn Abbas)

chapters.heading: From the Prophet of Mercy
chapters.body: During the truce with Quraysh, the Prophet ﷺ began writing to the rulers around him. Ibn Hisham lists the envoys and the kings: Dihya al-Kalbi to Caesar, king of the Romans; Abdullah ibn Hudhafa al-Sahmi to Kisra, king of Persia; Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri to the Negus of Abyssinia; Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a to al-Muqawqis of Alexandria; and others to the rulers of Oman, al-Yamama, Bahrain and the Syrian frontier (vol. 2, p. 607). The letter to Heraclius is preserved in the Sahih: it greets those who follow guidance, calls him to Islam, promises that if he accepts he will be safe and Allah will give him his reward twice, and warns that if he turns away the sin of his people (the 'tillers') is on him, and it ends by calling the People of the Scripture to worship Allah alone (Bukhari 2941). The same hadith, from Abu Sufyan, tells how Heraclius, at Ilya (Jerusalem), had Abu Sufyan, who was in Syria on trade during the truce, summoned and questioned him through an interpreter about the Prophet's ﷺ lineage, his followers, whether he had been known to lie, and his teachings (Bukhari 2941). In Bukhari 64 (Ibn Abbas) a letter was sent to the governor of Bahrain, who passed it to Kisra; he read it and tore it. The sub-narrator Ibn Shihab thinks Ibn al-Musayyab said the Prophet ﷺ prayed that Allah would tear them to pieces. This story does not follow what the other rulers did with their letters.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ wrote 'become Muslim and you will be safe' to the most powerful men alive. What does that tell you about the mission — fear, or invitation?

title: The Conquest of Makkah
subtitle: Eight years after being driven out — he enters with his head bowed
sources: Qur'an 110 — 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest'
Qur'an 17:81 — 'Truth has come, and falsehood has departed'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4280 — Abu Sufyan sees the Muslim forces pass; Sa'd ibn Ubada's words and the Prophet's reply; the flag at al-Hajun
Sahih al-Bukhari 4281 — reciting Surat al-Fath on his she-camel (Abdullah ibn Mughaffal)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4287 — the 360 idols around the Ka'bah (Abdullah ibn Mas'ud)
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 388-390, 399-400, 406-413 — the cause, the march, the entry, the orders, the address, the pictures

chapters.heading: The Day of Mercy
chapters.body: In Ramadan of the eighth year, Ibn Ishaq says, the conquest came, and that the Prophet ﷺ left Madinah on the tenth of Ramadan and camped at Marr al-Zahran with ten thousand Muslims (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 pp. 399-400). The immediate cause, in his account, was that Banu Bakr, who were in Quraysh's treaty, attacked Khuza'a, who were in the Prophet's, with Quraysh supplying them with weapons and some of them fighting in the dark (pp. 389-390). Bukhari 4280 has Abu Sufyan watching the Muslim forces pass. In that hadith Sa'd ibn Ubada, carrying the Ansar's banner, says 'Today is the day of a great battle', and the Prophet ﷺ answers that Sa'd was mistaken: today Allah will exalt the Ka'bah and it will be covered with its cloth (Bukhari 4280). Ibn Ishaq gives a similar report of Sa'd's words, that Umar told the Prophet ﷺ, and that the Prophet ﷺ had Ali take the banner from Sa'd (pp. 406-407). The Prophet ﷺ had ordered his commanders to fight only those who fought them, but named a few individuals who were to be killed even if found at the Ka'bah (p. 409); Abdullah ibn Sa'd was pardoned after Uthman asked for him, and Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl after his wife Umm Hakim asked for him and then brought him back to Islam (pp. 409-410). The army went in by separate roads. Ibn Hisham gives the Prophet's ﷺ address to Quraysh: he asked what they thought he would do with them, they answered with kindness, and he said: 'Go, for you are the freed ones' (p. 412). He ordered the pictures in the House effaced (p. 413). Surah An-Nasr speaks of that victory: 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes' and then to 'ask forgiveness of Him. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance' (110:1-3). Abdullah ibn Mughaffal saw him that day on his she-camel reciting Surat al-Fath in a quavering tone (Bukhari 4281). Around the Ka'bah were 360 idols; he struck them with a stick in his hand, saying 'Truth has come and falsehood has departed' (Bukhari 4287; Qur'an 17:81).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: He entered the city that tried to kill him and said 'you are free.' Who in your life deserves amnesty you have the power to give?

title: Hunayn and Taif
subtitle: Victory at Hunayn, and a city that later came to Islam
sources: Qur'an 9:25-27 — 'Allah has already given you victory in many regions'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4333 — Hunayn, the spoils and the Prophet's ﷺ words to the Ansar (Anas)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 — 'I hope that Allah will let them beget children who will worship Allah alone'
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 437-439, 478, 484, 499-500, 537 — Hawazin at Hunayn, Ta'if, the Ansar's reply, the delegation of Thaqif

chapters.heading: The Spoils and the Sweetness
chapters.body: After Makkah came Hunayn, against Hawazin and their allies under Malik ibn Awf, who had brought their property, women and children with them to Awtas (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, pp. 437-438). The Qur'an speaks of the day when the Muslims' numbers pleased them yet availed them nothing, and of Allah sending down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and the believers (9:25-27); in the hadith Anas says the Prophet ﷺ met Hawazin with ten thousand men besides the Tulaqa', the Muslims fled, he called the Ansar, who answered that they were at his command, and the pagans were then defeated (Bukhari 4333). He gave the spoils to the Tulaqa' (the recently converted Makkans) and the Muhajirun, and nothing to the Ansar, who were dissatisfied. He gathered them in a leather tent and said: are you not pleased that the people return with sheep and camels while you return with the Messenger of Allah? And if the people walked one path and the Ansar another, he would take the Ansar's path (Bukhari 4333; the Ansar's reply is not in that report). In Ibn Ishaq's account the Ansar wept until their beards were wet and said, 'We are pleased with the Messenger of Allah as our share and portion' (vol. 2 pp. 499-500). Then the Prophet ﷺ marched to Ta'if, where the defeated Thaqif had shut their gates (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, p. 478). During the siege he told Abu Bakr his dream of a bowl of butter that a rooster pecked and spilled; when Khuwayla asked for the jewellery of two Thaqif women if the city fell, he said he had not been given permission regarding Thaqif; Umar asked whether he had not been permitted, he said no, and Umar gave the call to depart, so the army left without taking the city (vol. 2, p. 484). In Ramadan of the ninth year, after Tabuk, a delegation of Thaqif came to him and they accepted Islam (vol. 2, p. 537). The hope he voiced on the day Ibn Abd Yalil turned him away — that Allah would let them beget children who would worship Allah alone — is recorded in Bukhari 3231.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Ansar were offered 'the Messenger of Allah' instead of wealth — and wept with joy. What would you take in place of money?

title: Tabuk
subtitle: The hardest march — and the hypocrites unmasked
sources: Qur'an 9:38-59 — the whole passage of the expedition
Qur'an 9:92 — those who came for mounts and wept
Qur'an 9:117-118 — 'Then He turned to them so they could repent'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4418 — Ka'b ibn Malik's account of Tabuk and the three who stayed behind
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 515-518 — the order to prepare for Tabuk, al-Jadd, those who held back, the weepers

chapters.heading: The Expedition of Hardship
chapters.body: In the heat of the ripening fruit season, with the shade pleasant and the journey long, the Prophet ﷺ ordered the Muslims to prepare to fight the Romans — Tabuk, in the year nine. He rarely named his destination ahead of time; this time he made it clear, because of the distance, the hardship and the size of the enemy (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, p. 516; Bukhari 4418). Al-Jadd ibn Qays asked to be excused, saying he feared he could not resist the women of Banu al-Asfar, and the Prophet ﷺ let him stay; the Qur'an says of such a man, 'Permit me [to remain at home] and do not put me to trial'; unquestionably, into trial they have fallen (9:49), and some hypocrites told one another not to march in the heat, which the Qur'an answers in 9:81-82 (vol. 2, pp. 516-517). The Qur'an warned in Surah At-Tawbah: 'If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and will replace you with another people' (9:39). Ibn Ishaq says he urged the wealthy to spend and that Uthman ibn Affan spent more than anyone (vol. 2 p. 518); seven men who came asking for mounts were told he had none, and went back with their eyes overflowing with tears (p. 518; Qur'an 9:92). In Ka'b ibn Malik's own account, something over eighty men gave excuses and oaths, which the Prophet ﷺ accepted; Ka'b and two others, Murara ibn al-Rabi' and Hilal ibn Umayya, were left pending. The Prophet ﷺ ordered the Muslims not to speak to the three, and it lasted fifty nights, until at dawn on the fiftieth morning a voice announced that their repentance had been accepted (Bukhari 4418; the Qur'an: 9:118, 'the three who were left behind ... Then He turned to them so they could repent'). Ka'b adds that the verse refers to the deferral of their case. As a reflection: three believers who stayed behind without a valid excuse were shunned for fifty nights, and when they were forgiven their repentance was written into the Qur'an.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Ka'b ibn Malik's punishment became a verse of forgiveness. What mistake of yours could become your testimony?

title: The Farewell Sermon
subtitle: At Arafat in the tenth year — life, property, honour, trusts and the rights of women
sources: Sahih Muslim 1218 — Jabir's account of the Prophet's ﷺ Hajj and the Arafat address
Sahih al-Bukhari 67 — the sermon on the Day of Sacrifice: lives, wealth and honour sacred; the present must tell the absent (Abu Bakra)
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 602-605 — the sermon as Ibn Ishaq gives it and who repeated it aloud

chapters.heading: Listen Well, for I May Not Meet You Again Here
chapters.body: Jabir ibn Abdullah says the Prophet ﷺ stayed nine years in Madinah without performing Hajj, then announced in the tenth year that he would go (Muslim 1218). At Arafat, after the sun had passed its height, he came down to the bottom of the valley on his she-camel al-Qaswa and addressed the people: 'Verily your blood and your property are as sacred and inviolable as the sacredness of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this town of yours.' He abolished everything of the Days of Ignorance, including their blood-revenges, beginning with that of the son of Rabi'a ibn al-Harith, and their usury, beginning with that of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib; told them to fear Allah concerning women, who have rights over the men as the men have rights over them; and said that he had left among them the Book of Allah, which, if they held fast to it, would keep them from going astray. Then he asked what they would say when asked about him; they answered that they bore witness that he had conveyed the message, discharged his trust and given sincere counsel; and he raised his forefinger to the sky, pointed it at the people and said three times, 'O Allah, be witness' (Muslim 1218). Ibn Ishaq gives a longer version that begins, 'Listen to my words, for I do not know whether I will meet you again after this year in this place', and includes: return trusts to those who gave them; no usury, but you keep your capital; every Muslim is the brother of every Muslim; and it ends, 'O Allah, have I conveyed?' The people said yes, and he said, 'O Allah, be witness' (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 pp. 602-604). In that account Rabi'a ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf repeated his words aloud to the crowd (p. 605). A separate hadith has him preaching on the Day of Sacrifice, on his camel, that blood, property and honour are sacred to one another like the day, month and city, and that those present must tell those absent (Bukhari 67, from Abu Bakra).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: He said every Muslim is the brother of every Muslim, and that blood and property are sacred. Whose rights might you be overlooking right now without noticing?

title: The Passing of the Prophet ﷺ
subtitle: The house of Aisha, the sword of Umar, and the steadiness of Abu Bakr
sources: Qur'an 3:144 — 'if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels [to unbelief]'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4437 — Aisha: 'with the Highest Companion'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3668 — Umar's denial, Abu Bakr's words and recitation, and the pledge to Abu Bakr
Sahih Muslim 1162 — fasting on Mondays: the day he was born
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 642-656 — the illness and the day of his death

chapters.heading: Monday
chapters.body: After the farewell pilgrimage and the sending of Usama's army, the illness began, in the last nights of Safar or the start of Rabi' al-Awwal according to Ibn Ishaq, after a night visit to pray for the dead of al-Baqi' (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 642); he went round his wives and, when the illness grew heavy in the house of Maymuna, asked their leave to be nursed in the house of Aisha, and they agreed (p. 643). When he fell ill he ordered that Abu Bakr lead the people in prayer (vol. 2, p. 652). On Monday, the day God took him, he lifted the curtain and stood at the door of Aisha's room while the people prayed Subh, and smiled at them; in another report on the same page Abu Bakr was leading and stepped back, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed seated beside him (vol. 2, p. 653). As his last moments came, with his head on Aisha's thigh, he said, 'O Allah, with the Highest Companion' (Bukhari 4437); The Prophet ﷺ died in the house of Aisha, on her day. Ibn Hisham has Aisha say he died between her chest and her throat (vol. 2 p. 655). Umar stood and refused to believe it: he has not died; he has gone to his Lord as Musa went, and will return (vol. 2, p. 655; Bukhari 3668). Abu Bakr came from al-Sunh, uncovered the Prophet's ﷺ face, kissed him and praised him in life and death, and told the people: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worshipped Allah, Allah is living and never dies — then he recited 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him' (3:144) (Bukhari 3668). Ibn Ishaq has Abu Hurayra relate that Umar later said that when he heard Abu Bakr recite it, his legs would not carry him and he fell to the ground, knowing that the Prophet ﷺ had died (vol. 2 p. 656). The Ansar gathered at the shed of Banu Sa'ida to discuss leadership, and Umar pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr and the people followed (Bukhari 3668). He died on that Monday, as the forenoon grew strong (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 654). Asked about fasting on Mondays, he had said it was the day he was born (Muslim 1162).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Umar denied it; Abu Bakr recited Qur'an. When grief hits your family, which one will you be?

title: What He Left
subtitle: No palace, no hoard, no empire in his name — and an ummah that outlives empires
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2739 — the Prophet ﷺ left no money, only his mule, his weapons and a charitable land endowment
Sahih al-Bukhari 3092 — 'what we leave is charity'; Abu Bakr and Fatima's request; Khaybar and Fadak
Sahih al-Bukhari 2068 — grain bought on credit from a Jew with his armour as a pledge
Sunan Ibn Majah 2697 — the last counsel: the prayer (da'if per Darussalam; al-Albani and al-Arna'ut grade it higher)

chapters.heading: The Inventory of a Prophet
chapters.body: When he died he left no money, no male or female slave, and nothing but his white mule, his weapons, and a piece of land he had given in charity (Sahih al-Bukhari 2739). He had bought food grain from a Jew on credit and given his iron armour as a pledge (Sahih al-Bukhari 2068). A report preserves his last counsel as: the prayer, and those whom your right hands possess (Ibn Majah 2697, graded da'if by Darussalam, while al-Albani and al-Arna'ut grade it higher). He left no inheritance to divide: 'Our property will not be inherited; whatever we leave is sadaqa' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3092). Abu Bakr cited those words when Fatima asked for her share of what he had left at Khaybar, Fadak and Madinah, and he declined to give it, saying he would not abandon anything the Prophet ﷺ used to do for fear of going astray; Umar later handed the Madinah charity to Ali and al-Abbas to manage and kept Khaybar and Fadak in the ruler's care (Bukhari 3092). As a reflection: the inventory is short: a mule, weapons, a plot given away, and a message.

familyQuestion: He left a mule, his weapons and a charity, and a message. What will your children inherit from you that money can't buy?

title: Reflections: The Man Who Walked Beside Us
subtitle: Thirty chapters, one walk — what it means to follow him ﷺ
sources: Musnad Ahmad — 'I have only been sent to perfect noble character' (number not verified)
Sahih Muslim 45 — none of you truly believes until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself
Qur'an 33:21 — 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allah often'

chapters.heading: The Example
chapters.body: The Qur'an does not say the Prophet ﷺ was perfect so you could worship him. It says: 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allah often' (33:21) — what the Arabic calls uswa hasana. An example is for following. He was an orphan, so the orphan is honored. He was a merchant, so the scale is straight. He was driven from his city, so the stranger is sheltered. He was driven out of Ta'if, so the rejected are comforted. He conquered, so the conquered are forgiven. He ruled, so rulers are accountable. He died poor, so the poor are honored. Thirty chapters walked past like thirty footsteps — and the invitation of every one of them is the same: walk here. Not in his century, but in his character. One way to answer the question — what did he leave us? — is: nothing you can hold, and everything you can become.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Thirty chapters end here. Which single habit of his ﷺ — honesty, gentleness, patience, courage, mercy — will your family practice together this week?

title: Iqra — The First Word
subtitle: The first word of the final message was not 'believe' or 'obey' — it was 'read'
sources: Qur'an 96:1-5 — 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — the beginning of revelation in the cave of Hira, 'I do not know how to read', and Khadija's words (Aisha)

chapters.heading: A Cave, a Covering, a Voice
chapters.body: Muhammad ﷺ used to go into seclusion in the cave of Hira, worshipping there for many days at a time, taking provisions with him and returning to Khadija for more, until the truth came to him suddenly while he was in the cave (Bukhari 3, from Aisha). The angel came and said, 'Read.' He answered, 'I do not know how to read.' The angel caught him and pressed him until he could bear it no more, released him and told him to read a second time; he gave the same answer; and it happened a third time. Then the angel recited the opening verses, beginning 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created' (96:1; Bukhari 3). As a reflection: the man who said 'I cannot read' was given, first, a command to read.

chapters.heading: The Name of Your Lord
chapters.body: The revelation that followed the command reads: 'Recite in the name of your Lord who created - Created man from a clinging substance. Recite, and your Lord is the most Generous - Who taught by the pen - Taught man that which he knew not' (96:1-5). As a reflection: the verses begin with the name of the Lord, and only then speak of knowing and of the pen, so every act of learning can begin with whose name is on it.

chapters.heading: What the First Word Decided
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ went back to Khadija with his heart beating hard and asked to be covered; once his fear had passed he told her everything and said he feared for himself, and she answered: 'Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your kin, you carry the burdens of the weak, you give to the one who has nothing, you honor the guest, and you help in the calamities that befall in the cause of truth' (Bukhari 3). As a reflection: the first revelation did not say 'rule', 'conquer' or 'gather followers'; it said read, in the name of your Lord. The first word turned to knowledge and the first home to comfort.

familyQuestion: What are we 'reading' in our home this month — and in whose name do we begin?
